notes: [HWF]: the pipeline (Verilator to C++, compile and instrument, mutate, keep coverage-increasing tests, discard the rest, save crashes; Fig. 3), the claim that software coverage correlates with hardware coverage (Fig. 13 caption and Section III-A), the oracle limit (Section VII-4: no hardware sanitizer, so invariants or a golden model; assertion violations and golden-model mismatches raise SIGABRT, Section VII-1), the harness (Algorithm 1), the bus instruction format (Fig. 4, Table I: opcode, address, data, with wait, read and write), the variable-frame result and its AFL reason (Section VI-B3, worded 'seem to perform better' in the paper), the reset result (Section V-C2: only the 8 and 16 state locks differ at p<0.05), the instrumentation result (Section V-C1: DUT-only never handicaps the fuzzer, better for small DUTs), the two-orders-of-magnitude result against the authors' own cocotb CRV bench for medium to larger locks (Section V-D), the 88 percent in one hour from an empty seed on three of four OpenTitan cores (Section VI-C, Fig. 14) and the analog and side-channel limit (Section VII-4) are each on the page as the document says.

[VArg] and [VLang]: --x-assign unique and --x-initial unique, the seed advice (use +verilator+rand+reset+2 and +verilator+seed+<value>, print the seeds selected, so a failure can be reproduced) and 'mostly a two-state simulator' are on the pages as the document says. Run locally on Verilator 5.052: with both options set to unique, the same +verilator+seed gives the same values for a never-reset register and an explicit X, and different seeds give different values. Imprecision: the document does not say that initial values only vary when +verilator+rand+reset+2 is given (without it the never-reset register read 0 on every run while the explicit X still followed the --x-assign choice); the VArg entry says to use it. The document says 'follows a seed given at run time', which is true with that runtime option.
